content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper deals with the problem of trusting data sources that can be more or less corrupt in the scenario where learning happens over multiple data sources (e.g. federated learning, multimodal learning). The paper provides an overview of variations of this problem and some fairly extensive literature review and proposes a method that assigns a level of trust to each data source. The method is based on the deviation of each data source from the average loss of the other data sources with a parameter controlling for the strictness of the condition over which a loss of trust is incurred. The gradients computed over each loss are scaled proportionally to the level of trust.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Good overview of the problem, a fairly simple method to implement. Easy paper to read and follow. 
On the other hand, the method is fairly heuristic and the overall contribution in terms of technical understanding of the problem fairly low.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear although the level of novelty is somewhat limited, I do think that it is quite easy (trivial) to come up with a method like the one proposed in the paper. It should be fairly easy to reproduce the results, and the paper is sufficiently clear and well written
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper provides a method that deals with learning from multiple sources of data while assuming that some are less reliable than other. While the method proposed is intuitive it is somewhat heuristic and could be very easy to come up with when faced with this type of problem. I do not think thus that this paper has the necessary technical contribution to be published at this venue.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of training a machine learning model with data coming from multiple sources with various qualities. The paper proposes a loss adapted plasticity method that dynamically adjusts the trust level of each data source and re-weight its impact on the model update based on the losses compared to other sources and over the history of training. The paper empirically shows that LAP has improved performance compared to a related method in the setting of federated learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper studies an interesting problem of learning from various sources, which have many practical use cases.
 
2. The proposed method is easy to implement and shows good empirical performance.

Weaknesses:
1. The paper does not define a clear objective to solve. I think it is critical to precisely define the problem of learning from various sources and have a notion of measuring the level of reliability of each source. This also helps to distinguish from existing settings such as noisy label learning and federated learning.

2. The proposed method lacks theoretical support. It is not clear why the trust level is updated in such a way, and why the tanh() function is chosen to re-weight the update based on the trust level. Overall, it is not clear that the proposed method can effectively identify the true qualities of each data source.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
The writing and the presentation of the paper are clear. However, the introduction is fairly short with limited motivation for the setting. The paper also lacks formal problem definitions and algorithmic descriptions.

Quality:
The empirical results are reasonable and trustworthy. However, I doubt if it is fair to compare to the baseline in the federated learning setting, where the global model cannot access individual training data samples.

Novelty:
The paper studies an important problem but the proposed method lacks principles.

Reproducibility:
The reproducibility of the paper seems solid.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper does not define the objective precisely and solves the problem in a principled way. Even though it shows promising empirical results using a simple method, I don't think the paper is ready be accpeted in its current form.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper describe a method of training neural networks from reliable and unreliable data. From the statistics of training loss from different source data sets, this method assigns a reliability score. Gradient gets updated 'more' on data set with a good reliability score (larger step size) and gradient gets updated less on a data set with poor reliability score.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. Description of the method lacks precision. This is a major weakness. See "Clarify, Quality, Novelty..." section of the review for details.
2. Gaussian assumption is not really needed (see last 3 lines of page 3). although if loss are multi-modal, Eq. (1) to Eq (3) may not work so well.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Encourage the authors to describe their work very precisely so that readers understand what exactly had been done. I give some examples here:
1.1. Section 4.2: "..the model becomes less plastic when..", need to define what it means to be "plastic"
1.2.How exactly are the losses over sources being feed in for training? are they being fed sequentially and hence there is a certain amount of forgetting? or are the sources being randomly picked with replacement to be fed into the training?
1.3. Eq.(3) R_{\xi} is a binary number? it takes +1 and -1 only? then clip at zero. or is R_{\xi} being incremented? For each source, are the R values changing over the training period?
1.4. Page 6, second paragraph "To implement the notion...in line with the perceived difficulty of the datasets." -- I read these text several times and failed to understand what is the main point of the text.
1.5. Fig3. "Original Data" means what? is this the original uncorrupted data?
 
2. There is little discussion on why by looking at the loss statistics alone, one can distinguish reliable and unreliable data. Good if there are some mathematical theory on this, otherwise a logical explanation will also help.
content.summary_of_the_review:
1. Description of method is not precise. Making reproduction of this work hard
2. Little discussion on the rationale of the proposed algorithm

content.title: Loss Adapted Plasticity: Learning From Data With Unreliable Sources
content.TL;DR: To learn from reliable and unreliable data sources, this paper demonstrates a technique that can be applied to any gradient descent optimiser: Update model weights as a function of the perceived reliability of data sources within a wider data set.
content.abstract: When data is streaming from multiple sources, conventional training methods update model weights often assuming the same level of reliability for each source; that is: a model does not consider data quality of a specific source during training. In many applications, sources can have varied levels of noise or corruption that can produce negative effects on the learning of a robust machine learning model. A key issue is that the quality of data or labels for individual sources is often not available to a model during training and could vary over time. A solution to this problem is to consider the mistakes made while training on data originating from sources and utilise this to create a perceived data quality for each source. This paper demonstrates a technique that can be applied to any gradient descent optimiser: Update model weights as a function of the perceived reliability of data sources within a wider data set. The algorithm controls the plasticity of a given model to weight updates based on the history of losses from individual data sources. We show that applying this technique can significantly improve model performance when trained on a mixture of reliable and unreliable data sources, and maintain performance when models are trained on data sources that are all considered reliable.
